capabilities.target: Supabase Postgres database via service role connection (bypasses row level security); includes the integration tokens table and all customers' ticket data
Insert rows into support_messages, rendered back to the customer who owns the ticket

inputs.source: Developer prompt in IDE client: 'Show me the latest open support tickets.'
Customer-authored ticket message submitted via the public support widget, stored in the database and returned by execute_sql reads

elements.name: Ticket message ingestion via SQL read
Insert into support_messages shown to customer
Supabase Postgres database (service role access, integration tokens table and support_messages table)

controls.name: IDE client per-call approval prompt showing the SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model, and shows the raw SQL text each call. Effectiveness decays with approval volume (approval fatigue), not model capability: developers approve many calls per session, and a crafted but plausible-looking query is easy to wave through.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role in place of the service role
controls.decay_rationale: A scoped, RLS-respecting credential would make the integration tokens table and other customers' rows unreachable regardless of model behavior, severing the injection-to-sensitive-read path.

controls.name: Injection classifier / sanitization on ticket message content
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier over ticket content catches common injection patterns but not adaptive, multi-turn payloads; narrows rather than severs the path.

controls.name: Insert target bound to the originating ticket record
controls.decay_rationale: Binding the support_messages insert target to the system-of-record ticket id, rather than a model-chosen target, constrains the sink even though it does not remove the underlying broad read access.

controls.name: Pin the Supabase MCP server package to a specific hashed version
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning counters rug-pull supply chain attacks where an update silently changes tool behavior after developers have already learned to trust the prompts; does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log with actor attribution
controls.decay_rationale: A structural, tamper-evident log distinguishing developer-approved from agent-chained SQL restores repudiation coverage; detective only, so it earns no residual tier credit.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): customer ticket injection + service-role read of integration tokens + exfiltration via customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Customer crafts a ticket message containing hidden instructions, stored in the ticketing table
Agent's execute_sql call (service role, bypasses RLS) reads the ticket including the injected instructions, and can be redirected to also query the integration tokens table or other customers' rows
Agent inserts the read data (e.g., tokens or other customers' content) into support_messages, rendered back to the customer who authored the injection

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: IDE client auto-approve/'always allow' enabled, per-call approval replaced with session-level approval, or approvals per developer per day rising above the low-volume threshold.

evidence.observation: MCP server launched with --access-token ${SUPABASE_PAT}; no credential scoping shown, consistent with service-role use.
The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security. A table of integration tokens sits in the same database.
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget. Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer.
The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL. Developers approve many calls in a session.

recommendations.action: Connect the agent with a least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role instead of the service role; deny access to the integration tokens table entirely.
Bind support_messages inserts to the system-of-record ticket id so the agent cannot write arbitrary content into an arbitrary customer-visible row.
Run an injection classifier over customer-submitted ticket content before it enters the agent's context.
Log every executed statement with an attributable actor tag (developer vs. agent-chained) distinct from the developer's own identity.

findings.title: No tamper-evident record distinguishing developer-initiated from agent-chained SQL execution

forecast.watch_signal: Session length or step count per task rising, making after-the-fact review harder without attribution.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit trail, or action-attribution mechanism is described anywhere in the configuration or runtime notes.

recommendations.action: Add a tamper-evident audit log recording the actor (developer vs. agent-chained call), the SQL executed, and the ticket context that triggered it.

findings.title: Unpinned Supabase MCP server package (@latest) enables silent tool redefinition and runs with full local OS privilege

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Package version string resolved by npx changes between sessions without an accompanying review, or the server stops matching a previously recorded hash.

evidence.observation: args include "@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest", pulled via npx with no version pin or hash, and no peer identity verification mechanism is described.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server package to a specific version and hash, and verify it before each session rather than resolving @latest at every launch.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe any identity verification between the IDE client and the agent process itself.
Artifacts do not describe step limits, spend caps, or rate limiting for the agent process itself.
Artifacts do not describe how customer identity is authenticated on the public support widget.
Ticket messages are written by an identified customer against their own ticket record; repudiation of the customer's own submission is not the concern assessed here.
This is an inbound flow from the public widget into the database; disclosure occurs on the outbound write leg, covered separately under flow.sql_write_reply_egress.
Artifacts do not describe rate limiting on ticket submission volume through the public widget.
Artifacts do not describe write-rate limits for inserts into support_messages.
Artifacts do not describe a rate limit or quota for the database behind the service-role connection.
Artifacts do not describe logging of MCP server-side actions or of package version changes over time.
Artifacts do not describe what the server process logs or transmits beyond executing SQL already covered under the database capabilities.
Artifacts do not describe rate limiting or resource bounds on the local server process itself.

rating.rationale: The agent connects to Supabase via a service-role credential that bypasses row level security and shares a database with an integration tokens table. Untrusted customer-authored ticket content is read by the agent (cap.sql_read) and can drive a write back into a customer-visible field (cap.sql_write_reply), forming a complete lethal-trifecta exfiltration path (ASI01/ASI02): inherent critical, residual high after the only declared control, a per-call approval prompt that shows raw SQL but is undermined by high approval volume (approval_review_mode raw_action, approval_volume high, giving one tier of credit rather than two). If that gate is removed or loosened (autonomy_increase, control_removal) the finding reverts to critical. Two further gaps compound the picture: no tamper-evident record distinguishes developer-approved from agent-chained database actions (property finding, high), and the MCP server package is unpinned (@latest) with no identity verification, exposing the design to a rug-pull supply-chain compromise (property finding, high). No single finding was found above low where no untrusted source reaches a sensitive sink today.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt or agent instructions text was provided; any prompt-level safety instructions are unknown and were not assumed to exist.

No logging, rate-limiting, or credential-scoping configuration was provided beyond what is stated in the runtime notes; absence of a control in the artifacts is treated as a design gap, not confirmed to be entirely absent in production.

The exact database schema (table and column names) is not provided beyond 'integration tokens table' and 'support_messages'; data sensitivity classifications are inferred from the stated purpose of each table.
